CausalChain: HCC metabolic reprogramming -> Elevated SAM/MTA production -> Epigenetic remodeling of T cells -> T cell exhaustion and increased immune checkpoints -> Secretion of chemokines by tumor cells -> Recruitment of TAMs -> TAM secretion of C5a and HGF -> Further suppression of T cell cytotoxicity and promotion of tumor progression -> Dual inhibition may restore T cell function and enhance immunotherapy.
Hypothesis: Simultaneous inhibition of dysregulated methionine metabolism in HCC cells and blockade of C5a receptor signaling in tumor-associated macrophages will synergistically reverse T cell exhaustion and improve immunotherapy outcomes in hepatocellular carcinoma.
Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is marked by a profoundly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) shaped by both intrinsic cancer cell metabolic reprogramming and extrinsic immune cell activity. In this setting, tumor cells display dysregulated methionine metabolism, leading to the accumulation of metabolites such as S‐adenosylmethionine (SAM) and methylthioadenosine (MTA) which can induce epigenetic modifications in infiltrating T cells, promoting their exhaustion and upregulation of inhibitory checkpoint receptors. Simultaneously, HCC cells secrete chemokines that recruit tumor‐associated macrophages (TAMs), which further support tumor progression, in part by releasing complement component C5a and hepatocyte growth factor (HGF), compounding T cell dysfunction. We propose that a dual therapeutic strategy targeting both the aberrant methionine metabolic pathway in HCC cells and the C5a receptor signaling in TAMs may synergistically reverse T cell exhaustion and restore effective anti‐tumor immunity, thereby enhancing the efficacy of immunotherapeutic approaches against HCC.
